Oscar Appeal

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's only been two week since Oscar Pistorius was released from prison under correctional supervision. Will his partial freedom be short-lived?

Summary:
It's only been two week since Oscar Pistorius was released from prison under correctional supervision. Will his partial freedom be short-lived?

When Judge Thokozile Masipa didn't find Oscar Pistorius guilty on murder last October, the NPA made no secret that they were bitterly disappointed. Jurors and legal minds across the country were suddenly confused about how exactly Judge Masipa interpreted the term dolus eventualis - that when firing the four shots through the toilet door, Oscar must have foreseen that he would kill someone. Even if he had no intent to kill Reeva on Valentine's night 2013, he must have foreseen that he would kill the person (according to his version, a burglar) behind the toilet door.

Further information:
Judge Masipa found Oscar Pistorius guilty of culpable homicide and sentenced him to five years in prison under section 276 (1) (i) of the Criminal Procedure Act - which would made him eligible to be considered for placement under correctional supervision after he had served one sixth of his sentence - in his case a time period of ten months.

At the time Judge Masipa delivered her verdict and sentence in October last year, the NPA already indicated that they would appeal her verdict.
The trial record and the State and Defence's Heads of Argument had to be handed in at the Supreme Court of Appeal in July, August and September this year and at the end of September the Appeal Court announced that the Appeal hearing had been placed on the role for one day, the 3rd of November, before a full bench of Judges.

The State bases its Heads of Argument on three main issues.

The State will argue in the Appeal Court that Judge Masipa didn’t correctly apply the principle of Dolus Evetualis – that when firing four shot through the toilet door, Oscar must have known that he could kill someone.

The state will also argue that Judge Masipa did not take into account crucial circumstantial evidence and ask whether she was correct to rely on one of several versions put forward by Oscar Pistorius - and to believe that that version could be reasonably, possibly true.

Pistorius’s defence, however, contends that Judge Masipa was correct in her decision - that Oscar did perceive some sort of danger, but that he lacked the intention to act unlawfully.

Oscar’s legal team will argue that the State is attempting to reintroduce its case of dolus directus – that Oscar killed with intent.

Judgment is likely to be reserved, but if the full bench of judges overturns Judge Masipa's verdict of culpable homicide and find Oscar Pistorius guilty of murder, he is likely to go to prison for 15 years. If this happens, Oscar's legal team is likely to appeal against this finding to the Constitutional Court.

If the Appeal Court Judges dismiss the State's Appeal, Oscar will serve out the remainder of his five year sentence under correctional supervision at his uncle Arnold's house. He will then be under correctional supervision until 20 October 2019.

Press Release:


Oscar Pistorius
This week state prosecutor Gerrie Nel argued before a full bench of Supreme Court of Appeal judges to have the culpable homicide verdict, decided on in the Oscar Pistorius Trial, overturned - and escalated to a murder conviction. Meanwhile Pistorius’s Advocate Barry Roux worked hard to convince the Supreme Court of Appeal that the High Court had not erred in its analysis of the intention behind the fatal shooting. With judgement reserved and Oscar Pistorius remaining under house arrest, Carte Blanche speaks to foremost legal minds for key analysis of these events.


Script:


OSCAR APPEAL SCRIPT
PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK
Just more than a year after the Oscar Pistorius murder-trial ended at the High Court in Pretoria, it was head to head again: chief State Prosecutor, Gerrie Nel vs defence advocate, Barry Roux. They became household names during the Oscar trial and this week they met at the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein.
JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: This is a very important case, it was a very strong bench, not only because there were five judges, but there were five senior judges.
The Supreme Court of Appeal is in a league of its own and very different from a High or magistrate’s court – it carries gravitas, and the judges are quite contentious, says retired Judge Fred Beckley, who sat on the Free State High Court bench for twenty-four years.
JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: I think the stress level is much higher in the SCA, especially a case is of national importance
But this case is also of immense importance to a family who lost their daughter. And the Steenkamps say it’s unlikely that the Appeal will provide them with the closure that they still long for.
As was the case during the trial, Reeva’s mother, June Steenkamp, supported by her best friend, Jennifer Strydom, arrived at the Appeal Court shortly before proceedings got underway.
But, in a recent interview with Carte Blanche, Reeva’s dad, Barry, said he wouldn’t be attending. He wanted to avoid the public eye and also only attended the verdict and sentence of the trial last year.
JOHN: Sitting in court and sharing that space with Oscar and other members of the Pistorius family, what was it like?
BARRY STEENKAMP: June and myself at times did feel sorry for them, for the family; with Oscar it was always just I don’t know its very difficult to explain it, inside yourself you would say all the time please let this get over and done with, but as you know, this, it just hasn’t come to an end.
The Appellant and Respondent in an Appeal case have to prepare and submit written arguments prior to the Appeal. These Head of Arguments are set out in much more detail than what their oral arguments would be.
The State’s appeal constitutes three issues:
- That Judge Masipa had erred in her application of the legal principle, Dolus Eventualis;
- That she incorrectly applied the legal principles pertaining to circumstantial evidence and multiple defences by an accused;
- And that the Judge was wrong to construct and rely on an alternative version of Oscar, and believe it could be reasonably, possibly true.
In answer to the State’s Heads of Argument, the Defence argued the following:
- That the State attempted to reintroduce its case of dolus directus – that Oscar killed with intent;
- That the State’s case rested on issues of fact rather than points of law; and
- The Defence contended that Judge Masipa was correct in her decision by finding that Oscar perceived some danger, but lacked the intention to act unlawfully.
JOHN LINK: Gerrie Nel kicked off by saying that the State’s Appeal was based on issues of law rather than fact. Having said that, he argued it is often difficult to separate the two, that one informs the other. In arriving at a verdict of culpable homicide, he said that Judge Masipa had ignored important circumstantial evidence.
Nel argued that Judge Masipa paid mere “lip service to the circumstantial evidence against Oscar”.
JOHN LINK: He mentioned for example the duvet and the jeans, the cellphone that Reeva Steenkamp took with her to the toilet on that fateful morning. Also the shouting that was heard by one of the so-called ear-witnesses, Estelle van der Merwe at about 2:30 in the morning or there about, and also the gastric contents that were discovered during the post mortem that was done on Reeva Steenkamp’s body.
GERRIE NEL: The court ignored the evidence, the most important circumstantial evidence that will make the accused’s version not reasonably, possibly true - impossible. If it did not happen as he described, how he woke up, how he walked, how he moved the fans, then it did not how she left the bed. But the court just ignored it and that is the most important fact.
Nel also argued that Judge Masipa ignored the evidence of the police’s ballistics expert, Captain Chris Mangena who reconstructed the toilet cubicle in court.
And Justice Steven Majiedt said he found how Judge Masipa dealt with Captain Mangena’s evidence, troubling.
JUSTICE STEVEN MAJIEDT: She finds that he is an excellence witness, and what if one reads the record it is quite impressive, but then you don’t understand how she gets to where she does in the fact that – she basically accepts what the accused said – that if he wanted to kill, he would have shot higher. …. Now, that is completely contrarary to Mangena’s evidence and his reconstructions.
Nel went on to argue that Oscar had multiple defences and that the court had relied on just one of them.
GERRIE NEL: He was not only a bad witness, he had defences that exclude each other and the one that he elected to use, the court rejected that one and gave him another one.
This decision by Judge Masipa, Nel said, effectively meant she had chosen a defence on Oscar’s behalf which was an error in law.
And Nel went on to argue that amongst Oscar’s conflicting defences, were that he opened fire because he perceived his life was in danger, saying he fired in reaction to a noise.
But Justice Nonkosi Mhlantla noted these were mutually exclusive.
VOICE OF JUSTICE NONKOSI MHLANTLA: Whilst he says I did not have the intention to shoot, he cannot rely on that defence.
GERRIE NEL: The court should have rejected his evidence as impossible, if the court took into account the circumstantial evidence, and the court should have rejected his evidence because he was a poor witness - then all that remains is the objective fact. On the objective facts, the accused cannot escape a conviction of murder.
JOHN LINK: The State’s appeal hinges on what it believes is Judge Masipa’s incorrect application of Dolus eventualis. That Oscar Pistorius in firing four shots into a small toilet cubicle must have known that he would kill someone. It was a theme returned to time and again by Justice Leach.
JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: All we got to call upon to decide is whether there were any misdirection – whether the finding should have been there was a person in this tiny cubicle when he fired four shots into that cubicle and that that constituted murder. Now, in that regards, do you ask that it is murder with direct intend – dolus directus or dolus eventualis.
GERRIE NEL: Dolus eventualis.
Gerrie Nel wrapped up his arguments after about an hour. And soon after Advocate Barry Roux started with his, he was questioned about whether or not Oscar shouldn’t have foreseen that by firing the shots through the door, he could have injured or killed someone?
JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: If you look at the photograpghs, there is room behind there for a toilet bowl, a person and just about nothing else. If you put a few shots through that opening, there is nowhere to hide, it would be a miracle if you didn’t shoot somebody.
Justice’s Leach’s line of questioning, was echoed by Justice Elizabeth Baartman.
JUSTICE ELIZABETH BAARTMAN: And he also knew there was no room to maneuver, then he put four, not one shot.
BARRY ROUX: For present purposes, I will accept that the person was not covered by the wall, and that by firing shots into the door, that the – at least - the possible consequence or the probable consequence would be that you injure a person and probably or possibly kill a person.
JOHN LINK: Barry Roux for the defence argued very strongly that Judge Masipa was correct to disregard Dolus Eventualis.
But Justice Leach said that Judge Masipa’s disregard of Dolus Eventualis was “just a misapplication”.
JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: Did he believe that he was entitled to shoot in those circumstances?
BARRY ROUX: There stands a man on stumps, he is vulnerable, he is extremely anxious, we see it now from eyes when we look back and we cannot do that with respect, we must take it in its totality, where this man is standing there and it starts before, where the anxiety started, when he is going to the bathroom, believing, incorrectly so that there is a problem.
JUDGE LEACH: I understand that.
JOHN: Even at this stage, do you think it would be fair to say, Judge, that Justice Leach seems to have a problem with how Judge Masipa interpreted dolus eventualis?
JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: He raised certain issues in the judgment of Judge Masipa which were very much in point, and I think with all due respect, they indicated that there was a bit of confusion in the mind of Judge Masipa when she gave her judgment and Justice Leach picked that up. Some of the issues that he raised were fairly important and I think they might have an impact on the eventual outcome of the case.
Judge Beckley says the Appeal should provide clarity on Dolus Eventualis. Judgment was reserved and it’s not clear when it will be delivered.
JUDGE BECKLEY: The majority judgment obviously will prevail. If the majority of the bench decide that the Appeal should be allowed, then that is the order that will be made and executed.
If the SCA upholds the State’s Appeal and replaces the verdict with one of murder, the case will be sent back to Judge Masipa for sentencing – this could take as long as two years.
JOHN: Most people would expect a 15 year minimum sentence, given that it is murder?
JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: Yes
JOHN: But that might not necessarily be the case?
JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: No, a 15-year sentence is just a minimum sentence, unless the trial court finds that there is compelling circumstances why a lesser sentence should be imposed – in such a case, the sentencing judge has a discretion.
But the Steenkamps say they’ll accept the outcome of the Appeal, whatever it is.
BARRY STEENKAMP: Whether they direct it the same way the case has gone, or their version that will come out of it, we will wait till then and we will go solely by what their judgment is to the case is.

JUSTICE STEVEN MAJIEDT: She finds that he is an excellence witness, and what if one reads the record it is quite impressive, but then you don’t understand how she gets to where she does in the fact that – she basically accepts what the accused said – that if he wanted to kill, he would have shot higher. …. Now, that is completely contrarary to Mangena’s evidence and his reconstructions. Nel went on to argue that Oscar had multiple defences and that the court had relied on just one of them. GERRIE NEL: He was not only a bad witness, he had defences that exclude each other and the one that he elected to use, the court rejected that one and gave him another one. This decision by Judge Masipa, Nel said, effectively meant she had chosen a defence on Oscar’s behalf which was an error in law. And Nel went on to argue that amongst Oscar’s conflicting defences, were that he opened fire because he perceived his life was in danger, saying he fired in reaction to a noise. But Justice Nonkosi Mhlantla noted these were mutually exclusive. VOICE OF JUSTICE NONKOSI MHLANTLA: Whilst he says I did not have the intention to shoot, he cannot rely on that defence. GERRIE NEL: The court should have rejected his evidence as impossible, if the court took into account the circumstantial evidence, and the court should have rejected his evidence because he was a poor witness - then all that remains is the objective fact. On the objective facts, the accused cannot escape a conviction of murder. JOHN LINK: The State’s appeal hinges on what it believes is Judge Masipa’s incorrect application of Dolus eventualis. That Oscar Pistorius in firing four shots into a small toilet cubicle must have known that he would kill someone. It was a theme returned to time and again by Justice Leach. JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: All we got to call upon to decide is whether there were any misdirection – whether the finding should have been there was a person in this tiny cubicle when he fired four shots into that cubicle and that that constituted murder. Now, in that regards, do you ask that it is murder with direct intend – dolus directus or dolus eventualis. GERRIE NEL: Dolus eventualis. Gerrie Nel wrapped up his arguments after about an hour. And soon after Advocate Barry Roux started with his, he was questioned about whether or not Oscar shouldn’t have foreseen that by firing the shots through the door, he could have injured or killed someone? JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: If you look at the photograpghs, there is room behind there for a toilet bowl, a person and just about nothing else. If you put a few shots through that opening, there is nowhere to hide, it would be a miracle if you didn’t shoot somebody. Justice’s Leach’s line of questioning, was echoed by Justice Elizabeth Baartman. JUSTICE ELIZABETH BAARTMAN: And he also knew there was no room to maneuver, then he put four, not one shot. BARRY ROUX: For present purposes, I will accept that the person was not covered by the wall, and that by firing shots into the door, that the – at least - the possible consequence or the probable consequence would be that you injure a person and probably or possibly kill a person. JOHN LINK: Barry Roux for the defence argued very strongly that Judge Masipa was correct to disregard Dolus Eventualis. But Justice Leach said that Judge Masipa’s disregard of Dolus Eventualis was “just a misapplication”. JUSTICE ERIC LEACH: Did he believe that he was entitled to shoot in those circumstances? BARRY ROUX: There stands a man on stumps, he is vulnerable, he is extremely anxious, we see it now from eyes when we look back and we cannot do that with respect, we must take it in its totality, where this man is standing there and it starts before, where the anxiety started, when he is going to the bathroom, believing, incorrectly so that there is a problem. JUDGE LEACH: I understand that. JOHN: Even at this stage, do you think it would be fair to say, Judge, that Justice Leach seems to have a problem with how Judge Masipa interpreted dolus eventualis? JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: He raised certain issues in the judgment of Judge Masipa which were very much in point, and I think with all due respect, they indicated that there was a bit of confusion in the mind of Judge Masipa when she gave her judgment and Justice Leach picked that up. Some of the issues that he raised were fairly important and I think they might have an impact on the eventual outcome of the case. Judge Beckley says the Appeal should provide clarity on Dolus Eventualis. Judgment was reserved and it’s not clear when it will be delivered. JUDGE BECKLEY: The majority judgment obviously will prevail. If the majority of the bench decide that the Appeal should be allowed, then that is the order that will be made and executed. If the SCA upholds the State’s Appeal and replaces the verdict with one of murder, the case will be sent back to Judge Masipa for sentencing – this could take as long as two years. JOHN: Most people would expect a 15 year minimum sentence, given that it is murder? JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: Yes JOHN: But that might not necessarily be the case? JUDGE FRED BECKLEY: No, a 15-year sentence is just a minimum sentence, unless the trial court finds that there is compelling circumstances why a lesser sentence should be imposed – in such a case, the sentencing judge has a discretion. But the Steenkamps say they’ll accept the outcome of the Appeal, whatever it is. BARRY STEENKAMP: Whether they direct it the same way the case has gone, or their version that will come out of it, we will wait till then and we will go solely by what their judgment is to the case is.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's only been two week since Oscar Pistorius was released from prison under correctional supervision. Will his partial freedom be short-lived?
metadata.Summary: It's only been two week since Oscar Pistorius was released from prison under correctional supervision. Will his partial freedom be short-lived? When Judge Thokozile Masipa didn't find Oscar Pistorius guilty on murder last October, the NPA made no secret that they were bitterly disappointed. Jurors and legal minds across the country were suddenly confused about how exactly Judge Masipa interpreted the term dolus eventualis - that when firing the four shots through the toilet door, Oscar must have foreseen that he would kill someone. Even if he had no intent to kill Reeva on Valentine's night 2013, he must have foreseen that he would kill the person (according to his version, a burglar) behind the toilet door.
metadata.Further information: Judge Masipa found Oscar Pistorius guilty of culpable homicide and sentenced him to five years in prison under section 276 (1) (i) of the Criminal Procedure Act - which would made him eligible to be considered for placement under correctional supervision after he had served one sixth of his sentence - in his case a time period of ten months. At the time Judge Masipa delivered her verdict and sentence in October last year, the NPA already indicated that they would appeal her verdict. The trial record and the State and Defence's Heads of Argument had to be handed in at the Supreme Court of Appeal in July, August and September this year and at the end of September the Appeal Court announced that the Appeal hearing had been placed on the role for one day, the 3rd of November, before a full bench of Judges. The State bases its Heads of Argument on three main issues. The State will argue in the Appeal Court that Judge Masipa didn’t correctly apply the principle of Dolus Evetualis – that when firing four shot through the toilet door, Oscar must have known that he could kill someone. The state will also argue that Judge Masipa did not take into account crucial circumstantial evidence and ask whether she was correct to rely on one of several versions put forward by Oscar Pistorius - and to believe that that version could be reasonably, possibly true. Pistorius’s defence, however, contends that Judge Masipa was correct in her decision - that Oscar did perceive some sort of danger, but that he lacked the intention to act unlawfully. Oscar’s legal team will argue that the State is attempting to reintroduce its case of dolus directus – that Oscar killed with intent. Judgment is likely to be reserved, but if the full bench of judges overturns Judge Masipa's verdict of culpable homicide and find Oscar Pistorius guilty of murder, he is likely to go to prison for 15 years. If this happens, Oscar's legal team is likely to appeal against this finding to the Constitutional Court. If the Appeal Court Judges dismiss the State's Appeal, Oscar will serve out the remainder of his five year sentence under correctional supervision at his uncle Arnold's house. He will then be under correctional supervision until 20 October 2019.
